newsitem.title: USA: BOXING-HOLYFIELD RETAINS WORLD TITLE WITH PRIDE INTACT.
newsitem.headline: BOXING-HOLYFIELD RETAINS WORLD TITLE WITH PRIDE INTACT.

text.p: Evander Holyfield woke up on Sunday still the World Boxing Association heavyweight champion, with his pride, if not his ear intact.
Meanwhile boxing, much maligned as violently out-of-date in an era of political correctness, received another black eye.

In one of the most sensational world title bouts in boxing history, pandemonium broke out as challenger Mike Tyson was disqualified on Saturday night for twice biting Holyfield's ears in the third round.

Before a sell-out crowd in the MGM Grand hotel/casino and an estimated 3 billion worldwide TV audience, police and security officials poured into the ring to keep the two camps apart. Tyson had to be restrained from going after Holyfield who he felt had deliberately head-butted him in the second round.
The champion ended what should have been a glorious night of triumph going to the hospital for surgery to try and reattach part of his right ear.

Referee Mills Lane's disqualification of Tyson before the start of the fourth round sparked calls from the Holyfield camp and from veteran boxing commentators to ban Tyson from the sport he dominated 10 years ago as the youngest world heavyweight champion ever.
"They should take his license away for life," said enraged Holyfield co-trainer Tony Brooks. "It was nothing but desperation (by Tyson). He had Evander alone and couldn't do anything."
Veteran ABC television sports reporter Dick Schaap echoed the thoughts of many who saw the fight."I have never seen that in boxing -- at the bottom of a rugby scrum maybe! They should ban him."
In fact, the Nevada State Athletic Commission will meet on July 1 to decide what to do about Tyson, who sometimes seems to lose all control.
The commission withheld Tyson's $30 million purse pending the meeting, at which it could fine him 10 percent of that amount or take even harsher action such as revoking his boxing license.
In Schaap's opinion, this was just what boxing did not need.
"This is a perfect death knell for the sport. Both their careers should end -- one (Holyfield) has nothing to prove, the other (Tyson) does this ..."
In fact, hidden in the uproar ending the fight was the fact that Holyfield -- together with Muhammad Ali, only the second three-time champion -- successfully defended his title against the odds.
Consecutive defeats of Tyson must have finally dispelled any doubts about the ability of a fighter who was a rank underdog in their first bout on last Nov. 9.
In that fight, the referee stopped the bout in the 11th round after Holyfield unleashed a barrage of punches against a weakening Tyson.
Yet Holyfield was still not favoured by the Las Vegas oddsmakers for Saturday's rematch despite a record that now stands at 34-3.
For Tyson, Saturday's bizarre behaviour was further evidence of the menacing fighter's lack of self-control.

This was his chance to prove that the "Iron" Mike Tyson, who was world champion in 1986 at the age of 20, was back. It was his chance to prove wrong the critics who said he had lost some of his intensity, as well as his killer punches after serving jail time for a rape conviction.
Yet Tyson, who says he has found spiritual peace after converting to Islam and who talks of the joys of fatherhood and a new marriage, oozed anger and hostility prior to the fight on Saturday.
Portraying himself as a victim of bad press, he closed his camp off to the media and snapped at reporters at pre-fight news conferences while giving monosyllabic answers.
In the ring on Saturday it seemed all the brooding and seething anger came to the surface.

Twice in the first round referee Lane had difficulty separating the fighters as Holyfield appeared to use his superior height and reach to tie up to the stockier challenger. Twice the champion connected with rights to Tyson's head and had him backing up to the ropes.
But it was in the second round that Tyson seemed to come apart after what Lane said was an unintentional head butt by Holyfield opened up a cut over Tyson's right eye.

He came charging out at the start of the third round and hit Holyfield with several aggressive left hooks. With 33 seconds left in the round the two were locked in a clinch in the centre of the ring when Holyfield suddenly leaped up and down and turned away from Tyson, his right ear dripping blood.
Tyson chased after him and gave him a shove in the back, prompting Lane to stop the clock, issue Tyson a warning and deduct one point.

After a doctor checked Holyfield's ear and said he would fight on, the two incredibly grabbed hold of each other again and once more Holyfield jumped in the air as Tyson's teeth ripped at his opponent's left ear.
This time the bell sounded and Holyfield went to his corner clutching his ear.
Before the fourth round could start, Lane disqualified Tyson, setting off some of the strangest sights ever in a sport event.
When it was all over, Holyfield was still the champion, Tyson awaits his fate and once again boxing fans are left shaking their heads about a once noble sport.
